pos: n. (the Austrian charterhouse of 1314, in the twentieth century the depot of unrestituted looted art)
etymology: German Mauer, a wall, and Bach, a brook; the walled stream.
biblical_def: Mauerbach west of Vienna was founded in 1314 by Frederick the Fair and was the principal Carthusian house of Austria until Joseph II dissolved it in 1782. Its later history is extraordinary. After the Second World War the Austrian republic used the buildings as the central depot for works of art looted by the Nazis whose owners could not be traced, and for decades thousands of paintings and objects sat in the former charterhouse while claims went unanswered. International pressure finally produced a 1995 law, and in 1996 the Mauerbach collection was auctioned in Vienna for the benefit of Holocaust survivors. This dictionary records Mauerbach for that long delay and its ending, because restitution is a biblical obligation with a schedule attached. Repentance is proved by giving the thing back, “If the wicked restore the pledge, give again that he had robbed” (Eze 33:15). Zacchaeus volunteers fourfold, “I restore him fourfold” (Luk 19:8). The law fixed the multiple, “he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep” (Exo 22:1), and required the principal plus a fifth, “that he shall restore that which he took violently away” (Lev 6:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines restitution as the act of restoring what was taken; to restore as to return to the owner; a pledge as something given as security; plunder as goods taken by force; and amends as compensation for an injury.
webster_full: RESTITUTION, n. The act of returning or restoring to a person some thing or right of which he has been unjustly deprived; indemnification.
RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former owner; to give back; as, to restore a stolen article; to repair; to make good.
PLEDGE, n. Something given or deposited as security for the performance of an act; a pawn; a gage.
PLUNDER, n. That which is taken from an enemy by force; pillage; prey; spoil; also, that which is taken by theft or fraud.
AMENDS, n. plu. Compensation for an injury; recompense; satisfaction; equivalent.
scriptures: If the wicked restore the pledge, give again that he had robbed, walk in the statutes of life, without committing iniquity; he shall surely live, he shall not die.
Luk 19:8
And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
Exo 22:1
If a man shall steal an ox, or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.
Lev 6:4

Then it shall be, because he hath sinned, and is guilty, that he shall restore that which he took violently away, or the thing which he hath deceitfully gotten, or that which was delivered him to keep, or the lost thing which he found,
corruption_summary: Austrian charterhouse of 1314: for decades after 1945 it held looted art whose owners could not be found, auctioned at last in 1996 for survivors.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture makes giving back the evidence of repentance rather than an optional sequel to it. Ezekiel names the restoring of the pledge as the first thing a turned man does, “If the wicked restore the pledge, give again that he had robbed” (Eze 33:15), and Zacchaeus does not wait to be assessed, “I restore him fourfold” (Luk 19:8).

The second thing is that the law set a multiple, which is uncomfortable because it means restitution costs more than the theft gained, “he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep” (Exo 22:1), with the principal and a fifth required in the case of a trust violated, “that he shall restore that which he took violently away” (Lev 6:4). A state that held other people's paintings in a monastery for fifty years while heirs died was not keeping a neutral position. The principle to recover is that delay in restitution is itself a form of keeping.

pos: n. (the first Carthusian house in Spain, founded 1194 in the Priorat of Catalonia)
etymology: Latin scala Dei, the ladder of God, from the ladder of Jacob's dream.
biblical_def: Scala Dei in the Catalan Priorat was founded in 1194 by Alfonso II of Aragon and was the first charterhouse in Spain; the surrounding wine district still takes its name, Priorat, from the priory. The name is traditionally explained by a story that a local shepherd told of seeing angels going up and down a ladder of light on the mountain, which is a retelling of Jacob's dream rather than an independent vision. The house was burnt and abandoned in the suppression of 1835 and stands in ruins. This dictionary records Scala Dei for the dream it is named from, because that dream is interpreted in the New Testament and the interpretation is the point. Jacob sees a ladder set between earth and heaven, “behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven” (Gen 28:12). He wakes afraid and names the place, “this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven” (Gen 28:17). And the Lord applies the whole image to himself, “ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man” (Joh 1:51), since there is one mediator, “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ladder as a frame with steps for ascending; a vision as something seen otherwise than by ordinary sight; a dream as the thoughts of a person in sleep; a mediator as one who intervenes between parties; and a gate as a large door or entrance.
webster_full: LADDER, n. A frame, usually of wood, consisting of two side pieces, connected by rounds inserted in mortises, by means of which persons may ascend a building.
VISION, n. The act of seeing external objects; sight; also, a revelation made to a prophet in sleep or trance; something imaginary.
DREAM, n. The thought or series of thoughts of a person in sleep; also, a vain fancy; an idle or wild conceit.
MEDIATOR, n. One that interposes between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them; by way of eminence, Christ is the mediator.
GATE, n. A large door which gives entrance into a walled city, a castle, a temple, palace or other large edifice.
scriptures: And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.
And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
Joh 1:51
And he saith unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
corruption_summary: The first Spanish charterhouse, 1194, named the ladder of God: its wine district still carries the priory's name, and the house is a ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ladder has already been interpreted, and the interpreter is the Lord. Jacob's dream is a real revelation of traffic between heaven and earth, “and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Gen 28:12), and his reaction is fear rather than delight, “How dreadful is this place!” (Gen 28:17). He names a place, and so did the Carthusians.

But Christ moves the ladder off the ground and onto himself, telling Nathanael he will see the angels ascending and descending on the Son of man, “and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man” (Joh 1:51). That settles two things at once. The access is real, and it is not located at a site or administered by a shrine, because there is exactly one mediator, “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). A shepherd's story on a Catalan mountain was a memory of Genesis; the ladder it described had a name by then.

pos: n. (the Castilian charterhouse near Burgos, founded 1441, with the royal tombs of Gil de Siloé)
etymology: Spanish mira flores, behold the flowers; from a royal hunting lodge of that name.
biblical_def: The Cartuja de Miraflores outside Burgos was given to the Carthusians in 1441 by John II of Castile, who made it his burial church. In the sanctuary stand the alabaster tombs of John II and his queen Isabella of Portugal, carved by Gil de Siloé in the 1490s in an eight-pointed star, together with the tomb of their son Alfonso and a vast gilded retablo. Isabella the Catholic commissioned the whole programme for her parents. The house is still a working charterhouse. This dictionary records Miraflores for its name, behold the flowers, because the Lord uses flowers to settle a comparison with exactly the kind of king buried there. He points at the lilies and tells his hearers to consider them, “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin” (Mat 6:28). The verdict on royal magnificence is unqualified, “even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29). The flower is also short-lived, “the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth” (Jam 1:11), and so is the man, “All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isa 40:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a flower as the blossom of a plant; a lily as a plant of several species with showy flowers; alabaster as a soft white stone used for ornaments; glory as splendour or magnificence; and to wither as to fade or dry up.
webster_full: FLOWER, n. In botany, that part of a plant which contains the organs of fructification, with their coverings; the blossom.
LILY, n. A plant and flower of the genus Lilium, of several species, remarkable for the beauty of their flowers.
ALABASTER, n. A sub-variety of carbonate of lime, a soft stone, white or variegated, used for ornamental vases and statuary.
GLORY, n. Brightness; luster; splendor; magnificence; also, praise ascribed in adoration; honorable fame.
WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its native freshness; to become sapless; to dry.
scriptures: Mat 6:28
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
Mat 6:29
And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
Jam 1:11

For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways.
Isa 40:6
The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:
corruption_summary: Castilian charterhouse of 1441, behold the flowers: the alabaster star-tombs of a king and queen of Castile, and a living community still.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the comparison the Lord actually makes. He does not contrast flowers with rags; he contrasts them with the richest king in Israel's memory and gives the verdict against the king, “even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29). The instruction attached is to look, “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow” (Mat 6:28), and to notice that the beauty is unearned.

The second thing is the brevity, which is the whole force of the figure and is lost when the verse is used as decoration. James watches the flower go in a single hot morning, “the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth” (Jam 1:11), and Isaiah applies it to flesh without exempting the eminent, “All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isa 40:6). A king in alabaster under a gilded retablo in a house called behold the flowers has been answered by his own address.

pos: n. (Bernard's second foundation, 1118, the most complete surviving Cistercian abbey)
etymology: From Latin fontanetum, a place of springs; French fontaine, a spring.
biblical_def: Fontenay in Burgundy was founded in 1118 by Bernard of Clairvaux, his second foundation, and moved to its present site in the valley of springs in 1130. It is the most complete Cistercian abbey surviving anywhere: church, cloister, chapter house, monks' hall, dormitory, infirmary, bakery, dovecote and forge all stand, the forge being among the oldest industrial buildings in Europe. Dissolved at the Revolution and used as a paper mill through the nineteenth century, it was restored from 1906 and is on the UNESCO list. This dictionary records Fontenay because what survives there is a pattern, and a pattern is a thing Scripture takes seriously. The tabernacle was built to one shown rather than designed, “look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount” (Exo 25:40), and the point is repeated, “According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle” (Exo 25:9). Hebrews says the earthly was a copy of something real, “See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount” (Heb 8:5). A form of words is likewise to be held, “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pattern as an original proposed for imitation; a model as a copy or representation on a small scale; a form as the shape or external appearance; a forge as a furnace where iron is wrought; and to imitate as to follow as a pattern.
webster_full: PATTERN, n. An original or model proposed for imitation; the archetype; an exemplar; that which is to be copied or imitated.
MODEL, n. A pattern of something to be made; a copy; a representation of something on a small scale; a standard.
FORM, n. The shape or external appearance of a body; also, a model; a draught; a pattern; manner; established practice.
FORGE, n. A furnace in which iron or other metal is heated and hammered into form; also, the work-place of a smith.
IMITATE, v.t. To follow as a pattern, model or example; to copy or endeavor to copy in manners and deportment.
scriptures: And look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount.
Exo 25:9
According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it.
Heb 8:5

Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Bernard's second foundation, 1118: the most complete Cistercian abbey standing, down to the forge, and a paper mill for a century before its restoration.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture repeatedly makes a pattern binding. Moses is not invited to design the tabernacle; he is shown one and told to match it, with the instruction given twice for emphasis, “look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount” (Exo 25:40), “after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof” (Exo 25:9).

The second thing is what a pattern implies about its original. Hebrews treats the whole tabernacle as a copy of a greater reality, which is why the exactness mattered, “See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount” (Heb 8:5). Paul carries the same idea over to doctrine, where the words themselves have a shape that can be kept or lost, “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13). Fontenay survives as the clearest surviving copy of the Cistercian plan; a dictionary is in the business of holding the form of words.

pos: n. (the Lower Austrian charterhouse of 1380, founded jointly by a lord and his wife)
etymology: From a Germanic personal name with Bach, a brook.
biblical_def: Aggsbach above the Danube in the Wachau was founded in 1380 by Heidenreich of Maissau and his wife Anna von Kuenring, who endowed it together and were buried in its church. Suppressed by Joseph II in 1782, it preserves one of the clearest Carthusian layouts in Austria, with the small cloister, the great cloister and the outline of the cells still readable, and the church serves the parish. This dictionary records Aggsbach for its founders, because a husband and wife acting as one in a large decision is the arrangement Scripture describes and the medieval record rarely shows plainly. The two are made one, “and they shall be one flesh” (Gen 2:24). A wife is a trust rather than a possession, “The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her” (Pro 31:11). Husbands are warned that their prayers depend on how they treat her, “that your prayers be not hindered” (1Pe 3:7), and the marriage covenant has God as its witness, “the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth” (Mal 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant as a mutual agreement; a wife as a woman united to a man in marriage; an heir as one who succeeds to an estate; to endow as to settle a fund upon; and conjugal as pertaining to marriage.
webster_full: COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; a stipulation.
WIFE, n. The lawful consort of man; a woman who is united to a man in the lawful bonds of wedlock; the correlative of husband.
HEIR, n. The man who succeeds, or is to succeed another in the possession of lands, tenements and hereditaments, by descent.
ENDOW, v.t. To furnish with a portion of estate; to settle a dower upon; to settle a permanent fund upon.
CONJUGAL, adj. Belonging to marriage; suitable to the marriage state; matrimonial; connubial.
scriptures: Gen 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil.

Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.
Mal 2:14
Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.
corruption_summary: Lower Austrian charterhouse of 1380: endowed jointly by a lord and his wife, who were buried in its church together.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unity Scripture asserts before it gives any instruction about roles. The two become one flesh, which is a statement of fact about what marriage is rather than advice about how to run it, “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife” (Gen 2:24). Proverbs then describes a husband resting the weight of his house on his wife's judgment, “The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her” (Pro 31:11).

The second thing is how seriously Scripture ties a man's treatment of his wife to his standing before God. Peter makes it a condition on the man's prayers, which is a startling clause to find in a chapter on submission, “giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel” (1Pe 3:7). Malachi names God himself as the witness to the covenant, which is why its breach is a matter of worship and not only of law, “the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth” (Mal 2:14). Two names on one foundation charter is a small testimony and a real one.

pos: n. (the Slovenian charterhouse of 1407, the only Carthusian house still living in the Slavic lands)
etymology: From Slovene pleter, wickerwork or a plaited fence.
biblical_def: Pleterje in Lower Carniola was founded in 1407 by Count Hermann II of Celje and was the last of the four Carthusian houses of the Slovene lands. It was abandoned in 1595 under Turkish pressure and the buildings decayed for three centuries; only the Gothic church of 1420 survived more or less whole. Carthusians returned in 1899, rebuilt the cloister and cells, and the house is the only living charterhouse in the Slavic world; its orchards and brandy support it. This dictionary records Pleterje for the single surviving church, because what remains when most is lost is one of Scripture's own governing ideas and it has a name. A remnant is left by God's doing, “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9). It is preserved on a specific principle, “Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5). It is said to be small and to be enough, “a remnant shall be saved” (Rom 9:27), and it is described as putting out roots again, “out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant” (2Ki 19:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a remnant as that which is left; a residue as the remainder; to preserve as to keep from injury; desolate as laid waste; and election as the choice of some to eternal life.
webster_full: REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part; the small part that remains.
RESIDUE, n. That which remains after a part is taken, separated, removed or designated; remainder; rest.
PRESERVE, v.t. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to defend from evil; to uphold; to save from decay.
DESOLATE, adj. Destitute or deprived of inhabitants; laid waste; in a ruinous condition; neglected; left alone.
ELECTION, n. In theology, divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy.
scriptures: Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
Rom 9:27
Esaias also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved:
For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and they that escape out of mount Zion: the zeal of the LORD of hosts shall do this.
corruption_summary: Slovenian charterhouse of 1407: abandoned under Turkish pressure, its Gothic church alone surviving three centuries, and monks back since 1899.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a remnant in Scripture is never an accident of attrition. Isaiah traces the survival of anything at all to God's act and says what the alternative was, “we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah” (Isa 1:9). Paul takes the word up and attaches it to a doctrine rather than to a demographic, “there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5).

The second thing is that smallness is not treated as failure. Paul quotes Isaiah on a people as numerous as the sand of the sea and a salvation confined to a remnant, “a remnant shall be saved” (Rom 9:27), and Hezekiah is promised a remnant that will go out and take root again, “out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant” (2Ki 19:31). One roofed church among ruins for three hundred years, and then a community again, is what the word looks like in masonry.

“out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant” (2Ki 19:31) — small, and sent out again.

pos: n. (the Mallorcan charterhouse of 1399, whose cells were let to lodgers after 1835)
etymology: Catalan vall de Mussa, the valley of Mussa, from an Arabic landowner's name.
biblical_def: The Real Cartuja de Valldemossa in the mountains of Mallorca was founded in 1399 in a former royal palace given to the Carthusians by King Martí of Aragon. The community was expelled in the Spanish suppression of 1835, and the cells were sold and let to private tenants; in the winter of 1838 and 1839 Frédéric Chopin and George Sand lodged in cell number four, where he worked on the preludes and she wrote a book complaining about Mallorca. The cells are now a museum. This dictionary records Valldemossa for the strangeness of that reuse, because Scripture has a lament for exactly this: a possession passing to people who have no part in it. Jeremiah states it in a line, “Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens” (Lam 5:2). The psalm asks for a dwelling to be left empty, “Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents” (Psa 69:25). Wandering is named as the judgment, “My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him” (Hos 9:17), and against it stands a possession no tenancy touches, “To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away” (1Pe 1:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an alien as a foreigner; a tenant as one who holds lands of another; a lodger as one who occupies a hired apartment; an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor; and dispossession as the act of putting out of possession.
webster_full: ALIEN, n. A foreigner; one born in or belonging to another country; one who is not a denizen or entitled to the privileges of a citizen.
TENANT, n. One who holds or possesses lands or tenements by any kind of right, whether in fee simple, in common, or for life.
LODGER, n. One who lives at board, or in a hired room; one who occupies a hired apartment in another's house.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; an estate which a man has by descent.
DISPOSSESS, v.t. To put out of possession by any means; to deprive of the actual occupancy of a thing, particularly of land or real estate.
scriptures: Lam 5:2
Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens.
Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents.
Hos 9:17
My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him: and they shall be wanderers among the nations.
To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,
corruption_summary: Mallorcan charterhouse of 1399: expelled in 1835, its cells let to tenants, one of whom was Chopin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the force of Jeremiah's lament, which is about dispossession and not about nostalgia. He does not say the houses were destroyed; he says they changed hands, which is harder to bear, “Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens” (Lam 5:2). The psalm's imprecation asks for the opposite outcome, an emptiness rather than a new tenant, “Let their habitation be desolate” (Psa 69:25).

The dictionary does not grieve the end of a charterhouse as such; its theology of the religious life is set out under the order's own entries. What it notes is the pattern. Hosea names the condition plainly and gives its cause, “because they did not hearken unto him” (Hos 9:17). And the answer Scripture gives to every dispossession is a holding kept out of reach of suppressions and leases alike, “reserved in heaven for you” (1Pe 1:4). A Carthusian cell with a piano in it is a strange sight and not the last word about anybody's inheritance.

Hebrew nokri (H5237) — a foreigner, an alien in the house; “our houses to aliens”, Lamentations 5:2.
Hebrew shamem (H8074) — to be desolate, left empty; “Let their habitation be desolate”, Psalm 69:25.
Hebrew shama' (H8085) — to hearken, which they did not; “because they did not hearken unto him”, Hosea 9:17.
Greek amiantos (G283) — undefiled, beyond reach of a lease; “To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled”, 1 Peter 1:4.
usage: “Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens” (Lam 5:2) — not destroyed, but changed hands.
“because they did not hearken unto him” (Hos 9:17) — the cause named plainly.
“reserved in heaven for you” (1Pe 1:4) — a holding no suppression touches.

pos: n. (the first Carthusian house in Castile, founded 1390 in fulfilment of a king's deathbed vow)
etymology: Spanish el paular, the marsh or pool, from paul, a boggy place.
biblical_def: Santa María de El Paular at Rascafría in the Sierra de Guadarrama was the first charterhouse in Castile, founded in 1390 by John I of Castile in fulfilment of a vow his father Henry II had made on his deathbed. It ran the first paper mill in Castile. Suppressed in 1835, it lost its celebrated cycle of fifty-four paintings by Vicente Carducho on the history of the Carthusians; the series was dispersed and was not reassembled in the monastery until 2011. Benedictines live there now. This dictionary records El Paular for the vow, because an inherited promise paid by a son raises the one subject Scripture treats most severely in this area. A vow is better not made than made and left, “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5). Delay is forbidden, “thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee” (Deu 23:21). God takes no pleasure in a slow payer, “defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools” (Ecc 5:4), and payment is made publicly, “I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people” (Psa 116:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vow as a solemn promise made to God; to perform as to carry out to completion; to defer as to put off; a legacy as a bequest; and obligation as the binding power of a promise.
webster_full: VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity; a solemn promise, by which a person binds himself to do or to forbear some act.
PERFORM, v.t. To do; to execute; to accomplish; to carry through to completion; to fulfil, as a promise or a vow.
DEFER, v.t. To delay; to put off; to postpone to a future time; as, to defer the execution of a design.
LEGACY, n. A bequest; a particular thing, or certain sum of money given by last will or testament.
OBLIGATION, n. The binding power of a vow, promise, oath or contract, or of law, civil, political or moral.
scriptures: Ecc 5:5
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee.
Ecc 5:4
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people.
corruption_summary: The first Castilian charterhouse, 1390: founded by a son to pay his father's deathbed vow, with the first paper mill in Castile.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how severely Scripture treats an unpaid vow. The Preacher does not merely prefer prompt payment; he says it would have been better never to have promised, “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5), and the law makes the delay itself the sin, “thou shalt not slack to pay it” (Deu 23:21).

The second thing is the characterisation of the slow payer, which is unflattering and deliberate, “defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools” (Ecc 5:4). Against that, the psalmist pays in public, before witnesses, which is the opposite of a private intention, “I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people” (Psa 116:14). Henry II of Castile promised a monastery as he died; his son built it. The dictionary does not hold that such a foundation buys anything, and it does hold that a promise once made is owed.

roots_lines: Hebrew nedar (H5087) — to vow, to bind oneself; “than that thou shouldest vow and not pay”, Ecclesiastes 5:5.
Hebrew 'achar (H309) — to delay, to be slack; “thou shalt not slack to pay it”, Deuteronomy 23:21.
Hebrew darash (H1875) — to require, to seek out a debt; “for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee”, Deuteronomy 23:21.
Hebrew kesil (H3684) — a fool, in whom is no pleasure; “for he hath no pleasure in fools”, Ecclesiastes 5:4.
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to pay in full, publicly; “I will pay my vows unto the LORD”, Psalm 116:14.
usage: “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5) — the severest word on the subject.
“thou shalt not slack to pay it” (Deu 23:21) — the delay is itself the sin.
“in the presence of all his people” (Psa 116:14) — paid publicly, not intended privately.

pos: n. (the charterhouse near Zaragoza, founded 1564, with Goya's murals of the life of the Virgin)
etymology: Latin aula Dei, the hall or court of God.
biblical_def: The Cartuja de Aula Dei north of Zaragoza was founded in 1564 by Hernando de Aragón, archbishop of Zaragoza, and is one of the later Spanish charterhouses. In 1774 the young Francisco de Goya, then in his late twenties, painted eleven large murals of the life of the Virgin on the walls of its church; four were destroyed after the 1835 suppression and the rest survive in poor condition. The Carthusians left in 2011 and a community of another order is there now. This dictionary records Aula Dei for its name, the court of God, because the courts are the object of some of the most direct longing in the psalms. A day there is weighed against a thousand elsewhere, “For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand” (Psa 84:10). The man who dwells there is called blessed, “Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee” (Psa 84:4). David reduces his desires to one, “One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after” (Psa 27:4), and the summons is answered with gladness, “I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD” (Psa 122:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a court as an open space before a house or an enclosure; a hall as a large room; a sanctuary as a sacred place; to dwell as to abide as a permanent resident; and praise as the commendation of what is worthy of honour.
webster_full: COURT, n. A space enclosed by walls and open above; also, the palace of a prince; the hall or chamber where justice is administered.
HALL, n. A large room at the entrance of a house or public building; a court of justice; a manor house.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple; also, a place of protection.
DWELL, v.i. To abide as a permanent resident, or to inhabit for a time; to live in a place; to have a habitation.
PRAISE, n. Commendation bestowed on a person for his personal virtues or worthy actions; the extolling of the Supreme Being.
scriptures: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Psa 84:4
Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee. Selah.
Psa 27:4
One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple.
A Song of degrees of David. I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Aragonese charterhouse of 1564, the court of God: Goya painted eleven murals there at twenty-eight, and seven of them survive.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the arithmetic of the eighty-fourth psalm, which is not pious exaggeration but a stated exchange rate, “For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand” (Psa 84:10). The psalm then goes further and prefers the doorway of God's house to a comfortable interior anywhere else, and calls the residents blessed, “Blessed are they that dwell in thy house” (Psa 84:4).

The second thing is the concentration of desire. David does not list his requests; he reduces them, “One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after” (Psa 27:4), and the object is to dwell, to behold and to enquire rather than to obtain. The pilgrim psalm then records the reaction to a simple invitation, “I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD” (Psa 122:1). A house named the court of God, painted by a young Goya and now in other hands, is still a good name for the thing the psalms want.

pos: n. (the Catalan charterhouse of 1415 near Barcelona, still a living community)
etymology: Catalan mont alegre, the cheerful or glad mountain.
biblical_def: Santa Maria de Montalegre at Tiana, north of Barcelona, was founded in 1415 by the union of two earlier Carthusian houses, Sant Pol de Mar and Vallparadís. It was sacked in the Napoleonic wars, suppressed in 1835, and reoccupied; it survived the burning of churches in the Spanish Civil War, when the monks were dispersed and some killed, and the community is there still, keeping the full Carthusian observance. This dictionary records Montalegre for its name, the glad mountain, because gladness in Scripture is commanded rather than merely permitted, and it is not the same thing as circumstances being pleasant. Joy is named as strength, “for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Neh 8:10). Its location is given, “in thy presence is fulness of joy” (Psa 16:11). It is a thing God himself effects by exchange, “Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing” (Psa 30:11), and it is twice commanded by an apostle writing from prison, “Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice” (Phi 4:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines joy as a delight of the mind from the consideration of good; gladness as joy or pleasure of the mind; to rejoice as to experience joy; mirth as merriment; and cheerfulness as a state of moderate joy.
webster_full: JOY, n. The passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; that excitement of pleasurable feelings which is caused by success or good fortune.
GLADNESS, n. Joy, or a moderate degree of joy and exhilaration; pleasure of mind; cheerfulness.
REJOICE, v.i. To experience joy and gladness in a high degree; to be exhilarated with lively and pleasurable sensations.
MIRTH, n. Social merriment; hilarity; noisy gayety; jollity; noisy laughter.
CHEERFULNESS, n. Life; animation; good spirits; a state of moderate joy or gayety; alacrity.
scriptures: Neh 8:10

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;
Phi 4:4
Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
corruption_summary: Catalan charterhouse of 1415, the glad mountain: sacked, suppressed, dispersed in the Civil War, and keeping the full observance still.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture makes joy a strength rather than a mood. Nehemiah says it to people who had just wept at hearing the law read, and he tells them to stop and eat, “for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Neh 8:10). The psalm locates it in a presence rather than in a set of conditions, “in thy presence is fulness of joy” (Psa 16:11).

The second thing is that the exchange is God's to make. David does not describe cheering himself up; he describes a reversal done to him, “Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing” (Psa 30:11). And the command to rejoice comes from a man under guard, repeated so that no reader can treat it as a remark about the weather, “Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice” (Phi 4:4). A house called the glad mountain that has been sacked three times has as much right to the name as anyone.

Hebrew machol (H4234) — a dance, exchanged for mourning; “Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing”, Psalm 30:11.
Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to turn, to overturn; “Thou hast turned for me my mourning”, Psalm 30:11.
Greek chairo (G5463) — to rejoice, commanded twice; “Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice”, Philippians 4:4.
usage: “for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Neh 8:10) — said to people who had just wept.
“Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing” (Psa 30:11) — a reversal done to him.
“Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice” (Phi 4:4) — written under guard, and repeated.
